ai.definition: Atom-by-atom assemblers are devices that can manipulate individual atoms or molecules to create complex structures, potentially leading to the construction of any material or device at the atomic scale.
ai.howItWorks: These assemblers utilize scanning probe microscopy (SPM) techniques and molecular robotics to directly manipulate atoms. They operate by moving an instrumented tip in close proximity to a surface, allowing for precise placement of individual atoms or molecules into desired positions.
ai.problemSolved: Current limitations in manufacturing precision, particularly at the atomic scale, where defects are common due to manual processes and equipment constraints.
ai.manufacturing: Theoretical concept; no practical implementation exists. Requires advanced nanotechnology and molecular robotics capabilities.
ai.buildProcess: Involves developing highly precise robotic systems capable of manipulating atoms with SPM techniques, integrating these with existing fabrication methods.
ai.costDrivers: High research and development costs, specialized materials for tip manufacturing, complex integration of micro- and nano-scale components.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term potential; currently in early theoretical stages but could revolutionize manufacturing if realized.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations exist due to the theoretical nature. However, once developed, safety and environmental guidelines will be necessary.
ai.risks: Technological challenges, high development costs, regulatory hurdles, and ethical concerns regarding misuse or unintended consequences.
ai.profitability: Uncertain; depends on successful commercialization of applications in various industries.
ai.futureDevelopment: Continued research into nanotechnology, SPM techniques, and molecular robotics. Potential integration with existing manufacturing processes.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and precise control systems.

glossary.def: A family of microscopy techniques that scan a probe over a surface to image the topography with atomic resolution.
The design and construction of robots at the molecular scale, capable of performing precise operations on individual molecules or atoms.

subsystems.name: Scanning probe head
subsystems.role: the working end — a sharp tip a few atoms across, held within a fraction of a nanometre of the workpiece.

subsystems.name: Positioning and metrology
subsystems.role: tells the system exactly where the tip is, and keeps it there.

subsystems.name: Tip chemistry
subsystems.role: makes the tip a tool rather than just a probe — reactive or catalytic.
parts: reactive atom or molecular fragment at apex

subsystems.name: Feedstock handling
subsystems.role: delivers the right molecules, one at a time, to the right place.

subsystems.name: Reaction control
subsystems.role: triggers bond formation and bond breaking at a chosen atom.

subsystems.name: Computational control
subsystems.role: simulates the reaction, plans the sequence and verifies the result.

buildSteps.title: Design the reaction
buildSteps.detail: Compute, atom by atom, which molecule will react with which, and what energy or pulse is needed to make it happen without side reactions.

buildSteps.title: Shape the tooltip
buildSteps.detail: Prepare a scanning probe tip, often by deliberately picking up a single molecule or atom to give it a known reactive apex.

buildSteps.title: Verify atomically
buildSteps.detail: Image the surface and the tip with the same instrument, so the operator knows exactly what is where before touching anything.

buildSteps.title: Place the feedstock
buildSteps.detail: Deposit a single molecule from the surface or the tip into a defined site, at liquid-helium temperatures that stop it wandering.

buildSteps.title: Form one bond
buildSteps.detail: Apply a local voltage pulse or force to drive a single bond-forming reaction at the chosen atoms.

buildSteps.title: Confirm and correct
buildSteps.detail: Re-image to check the product; if the reaction failed, remove the fragment and try again.

buildSteps.title: Repeat under automation
buildSteps.detail: Software sequences tens of thousands of such steps to build a small atomically precise object.

buildSteps.title: Scale the throughput
buildSteps.detail: Replace the single tip with arrays of thousands of independently controlled tips, or with self-assembling molecular machines that replicate the same chemistry in bulk.

prerequisites.why: scanning tunnelling and atomic force microscopy, developed from 1981 onward, are what make position-by-position work possible at all.
piezoelectric scanners already move and hold a tip to better than 0.1 nm at low temperature.
quantum chemistry can predict many reactions, but predicting the exact outcome under a probe tip is not yet reliable.
only a handful of specific, simple bond-forming reactions have been driven this way in the laboratory; general tooltips are unproven.

prerequisites.tech: Parallel tip arrays with error correction
prerequisites.why: one tip is far too slow to make anything useful; thousands working in parallel with automatic retries do not exist.
nothing yet shows how a finished, atomically precise object is detached, kept stable and used at practical scale.

pathway.milestone: single-atom positioning and imaging, first demonstrated by spelling a logo with individual atoms in 1989, plus molecular machines recognised by a Nobel Prize in 2016
pathway.unlocks: proof that atoms can be addressed one at a time.

pathway.milestone: routinely driving designed bond-forming reactions under a probe tip, and characterising the products
pathway.unlocks: a real toolbox of mechanosynthetic reactions.

pathway.milestone: parallel tip arrays building small atomically precise structures such as stiff rods, gears or graphene-like sheets
pathway.unlocks: demonstration that positional assembly can beat chemistry's usual messiness.

pathway.milestone: self-assembling or self-replicating molecular machinery that copies the same chemistry rapidly
pathway.unlocks: cheap, defect-free materials — or, if it proves physically impractical, a definitive answer that this route is a dead end.
